rows.title: Carney's 'ambitious' but 'risky' budget eyes investment in uncertain world
rows.fact: Canada's 2026 federal budget projects a deficit of C$62.3 billion for 2026-27, declining over the five-year plan. It adds C$151 billion in new supports over five years, including C$67 billion to attract business investment, such as a productivity 'mega deduction' allowing new investments to be expensed immediately. Core defence spending rises from C$75.1 billion in 2026-27 to C$99.2 billion in 2030-31.
rows.outlook: Desjardins chief economist Jimmy Jean called the budget 'very ambitious' but 'risky', warning that debt metrics would deteriorate if execution falls short.
rows.why: 정부가 적자를 감수하면서 투자와 생산성에 돈을 쓰는 '확장 재정'의 논리와 위험을 실제 예산 숫자로 따져볼 수 있다.
rows.term_def: When government spending exceeds revenue such as taxes; the gap is covered by issuing government bonds.
rows.note: The Globe and Mail also covered the budget, but its article could not be accessed, so the facts were verified through Global News's own reporting.
rows.why_en: It lets you weigh, with real budget figures, the logic and risks of expansionary fiscal policy, where a government accepts deficits to fund investment and productivity.
rows.summary: Canada's government has released its 2026 federal budget, projecting a deficit of C$62.3 billion for 2026-27 that is set to shrink over five years. It says better-than-expected revenue and tighter operating spending helped fund C$151 billion in new supports over five years. Of that, C$67 billion goes to attracting business investment, including a 'mega deduction' that lets firms expense new investments immediately, and core defence spending rises from C$75.1 billion in 2026-27 to C$99.2 billion in 2030-31. The budget assumes trade-war headwinds will be largely offset by stronger-than-expected economic performance earlier this year.

opinion.title: Budget 2026: Canada goes all-in on corporate profits
opinion.author: David Macdonald
opinion.summary: David Macdonald, senior economist at the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives, a progressive think tank, argues that Budget 2026 is mainly a corporate budget presented as a cost-of-living response. His main target is the productivity 'mega deduction', which by his own calculation sends 29% of its benefit to oil extraction and refining and 10% to mining, and which he says will often subsidize investment that would have happened anyway. He gives limited credit to income measures such as a one-time 50% boost to the Groceries and Essentials Benefit, which he estimates lifts about 120,000 people above the poverty line, but calls them temporary or incomplete.
opinion.why: 같은 예산안을 '투자 촉진'으로 보는 정부와 '기업 특혜'로 보는 비판을 나란히 읽으며, 세금 혜택이 실제로 누구에게 돌아가는지 따져보는 연습을 할 수 있다.
opinion.why_en: Reading the government's 'investment boost' case beside this 'corporate giveaway' critique trains you to ask who actually benefits from a tax break.

rows.title: U.S. employers added a surprising 165,000 jobs in October; unemployment rate dipped to 4.1%
rows.fact: U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs in October, far above the 65,000 economists expected, and the unemployment rate dipped to 4.1%. Average hourly earnings rose 3.1% from a year earlier, but the article notes that persistently high inflation means many workers have lost purchasing power. Yale's Budget Lab estimates the monthly job gain needed to keep unemployment steady has fallen to about 5,000, from roughly 166,000 in late 2023.
rows.outlook: Some economists expect the Fed to raise rates in December; CME FedWatch, as cited in the article, put the odds of a December hike at 77%.
rows.why: 고용 지표가 좋으면 왜 금리 인상 전망이 커지는지, 그리고 일자리 수만큼 노동 공급 변화도 중요하다는 점을 실제 숫자로 볼 수 있다.
rows.term_def: The monthly change in the number of U.S. jobs outside farming; a key gauge of the U.S. economy.
rows.why_en: It shows with real numbers why strong job data raises expectations of rate hikes, and why changes in labor supply matter as much as the job count.
rows.summary: U.S. nonfarm payrolls rose by 165,000 in October, far above the 65,000 economists expected, and August and September were revised up by a combined 84,000 jobs. The unemployment rate fell to 4.1% even though 421,000 people joined the labor force. Professional and business services (70,000) and health care (about 42,000) led hiring, while hotels, restaurants and bars cut 10,600 jobs. Average hourly earnings rose 3.1% from a year earlier, but the article notes that high inflation has left many workers with less purchasing power. The Fed raised rates in September and held them in October.

opinion.title: What a Hotter-Than-Expected October Jobs Report Means for the Fed
opinion.author: David Dittman
opinion.summary: Kiplinger investing editor David Dittman argues that October's hotter-than-expected jobs report strengthens the case for a quarter-point Fed rate hike in December. He points to payroll gains far above forecasts, upward revisions of 84,000 jobs for August and September, a dip in unemployment to 4.1% and stronger-than-expected wage growth. Futures pricing cited in the piece implied roughly a 73% chance of a December hike, though the analysts he quotes disagree on how far the Fed will go.
opinion.why: 좋은 경제 뉴스가 왜 금리 인상, 즉 대출 비용 상승으로 이어질 수 있는지 시장의 시각에서 이해할 수 있다.
opinion.why_en: It explains, from the market's point of view, why good economic news can mean higher interest rates and costlier borrowing.

rows.title: Consumer prices up 2.8% in October, remain in 2% range for 2nd month
rows.summary: South Korea's consumer prices rose 2.8% in October from a year earlier, down from 2.9% in September and 3.1% in August, keeping inflation in the 2% range for a second month. Petroleum product prices jumped 14.9%, with diesel up 19.7% and gasoline up 11.6%, while farm, livestock and fishery prices fell 1.7% for a third straight monthly decline. Dining-out prices rose 2.9%, the fastest since February, and core inflation excluding food and energy was 2.8%. The finance ministry estimates the government's fuel price cap lowered October inflation by 0.8 percentage points.
rows.fact: Consumer prices rose 2.8% year on year in October, with petroleum products up 14.9% and adding 0.56 percentage points to the headline rate. Core inflation, excluding food and energy, was also 2.8%. The finance ministry estimates the fuel price cap lowered October inflation by 0.8 points.
rows.outlook: The Bank of Korea expects November inflation to stay in the high-2% range, citing global oil prices and a continued upward trend in core inflation.
rows.why: 국제유가 같은 외부 충격이 국내 물가로 어떻게 전해지는지, 그리고 정부의 유류 가격 상한이 물가 지표를 얼마나 낮추는지 직접 확인할 수 있다.
rows.why_en: It shows how an external shock such as global oil prices feeds into domestic prices, and how much a government fuel price cap holds down measured inflation.
rows.term_def: Inflation excluding volatile food and energy prices; used to gauge the underlying price trend.
rows.note: The November outlook is the Bank of Korea's assessment as reported by Yonhap via The Korea Times (Nov. 3).

opinion.title: When the economic illusion fades
opinion.author: Cho Min-geun (JoongAng Ilbo editorial writer)
opinion.summary: Cho Min-geun argues that Korea's apparent recovery, with growth rebounding into the 3% range and inflation in the upper 2% range, rests on two props: government fuel price caps and a semiconductor export boom. He notes that the fuel price ceiling, now in its eighth month, has drawn more than 5.6 trillion won in budget money, and that chips accounted for 73% of this year's export increase and 49% of total exports last month. He warns that the cap is unsustainable without an exit plan and that reliance on chips leaves the economy exposed, and urges a credible 'plan B' and structural reform.
opinion.why: 정부의 가격 통제가 물가 지표를 낮추는 대신 재정 부담과 가격 왜곡을 남긴다는 점, 그리고 한 산업에 쏠린 성장의 위험을 함께 생각해볼 수 있다.
opinion.why_en: It shows that price controls can lower the inflation figure while leaving fiscal costs and distortions behind, and why growth that leans on one industry is risky.

rows.title: BoE hikes rate for first time in 3 years; retreating oil prices may allow for more options ahead
rows.fact: The Bank of England raised its key rate from 3.75% to 4% on Nov. 5, its first increase since August 2023. UK consumer price inflation reached 3.5% in September, well above the 2% target, driven mainly by higher fuel costs from the Iran war and supply disruption in the Strait of Hormuz. Eight of the nine Monetary Policy Committee members voted for a 0.25-point rise; one wanted 0.5 points.
rows.outlook: The bank expects inflation to peak at around 5% next summer, and Governor Andrew Bailey said the move should not be seen as the start of an inevitable long sequence of hikes.
rows.why: 에너지 가격 충격이 물가를 밀어 올리고 중앙은행이 금리로 대응하는 '공급 충격과 통화정책'의 관계를 가장 선명하게 보여준다.
rows.term_def: The interest rate set by a central bank; it influences lending and deposit rates across the economy.
rows.note: Rate, vote and inflation figures were checked against the Bank of England's official Monetary Policy Summary (Nov. 5).
rows.why_en: It is the clearest example of how an energy supply shock pushes up prices and how a central bank responds with interest rates.
rows.summary: The Bank of England raised its key rate from 3.75% to 4% on Nov. 5, its first increase since August 2023. The trigger was higher fuel costs from the Iran war and supply disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, which pushed UK consumer price inflation to 3.5% in September, well above the 2% target. A higher rate raises mortgage costs for households and borrowing costs for businesses. In the same week, Brent crude fell about $15 to $96 as fears of further U.S. strikes on Iran eased after the U.S. midterm elections.

opinion.title: Hawkish Bank of England hikes rates, and there's more to come
opinion.author: James Smith (ING economist)
opinion.summary: ING economist James Smith calls the Bank of England's move more hawkish than expected: a hike driven by risk rather than by inflation that is already spreading through the economy. He notes that the Bank's own forecasts show inflation, seen peaking at 4.9%, is almost entirely energy-driven, and that no data yet show the energy shock spreading across prices. He expects about half a percentage point of tightening in total, with another hike by February, and sees a good chance of rate cuts starting in late 2027 or early 2028.
opinion.why: 중앙은행이 '이미 오른 물가'가 아니라 '앞으로 번질 위험'에 대비해 금리를 올리는 보험성 인상의 논리를 이해할 수 있다.
opinion.why_en: It explains the logic of an 'insurance' rate hike, aimed at the risk of inflation spreading rather than at inflation already in the data.

rows.title: Japan's real wages rise for ninth month in September, backing BOJ rate hike
rows.fact: Japan's real wages rose 2.2% in September from a year earlier, the ninth straight monthly gain. Nominal wages (total cash earnings) rose 4.6%, the fastest since January 1997, partly reflecting a jump in one-off special payments that the government attributed to a statistical quirk; base pay rose 3.7%. The inflation rate used to calculate real wages was 2.4%.
rows.outlook: Reuters says the data strengthens the case for further Bank of Japan rate hikes, and many analysts expect the next hike as soon as December.
rows.why: 월급이 오른 비율에서 물가 상승률을 빼야 실제 생활수준의 변화가 보인다는 '명목 vs 실질'의 차이를 정확한 숫자로 익힐 수 있다.
rows.term_def: Nominal wage growth minus inflation; it shows how much more (or less) a paycheck can actually buy.
rows.why_en: It teaches, with precise numbers, the difference between nominal and real: subtract inflation from pay growth to see how living standards actually changed.
rows.summary: Japan's real wages rose 2.2% in September from a year earlier, the ninth straight monthly gain. Nominal wages (total cash earnings) jumped 4.6%, the biggest rise since January 1997, though that includes a surge in one-off special payments the government attributed to a statistical quirk. Base pay, a steadier measure, rose 3.7%, in line with August's 3.8%. The inflation rate used to calculate real wages was 2.4%, so pay outpaced prices. Reuters says the trend strengthens the case for further Bank of Japan rate hikes.

opinion.title: Japan Real Wages Accelerate to 2.2% as Base Pay Holds Firm, Supporting BoJ Hike Outlook
opinion.author: ActionForex staff
opinion.summary: This market commentary argues that Japan's September wage data supports further Bank of Japan tightening, but warns that the headline is flattering. Nominal earnings rose 4.6%, yet special payments jumped 32.6% on what the labour ministry called a statistical distortion, while scheduled base pay eased to 3.7% from 3.8%. The writer sees steady base pay and labour shortages as enough to justify another hike, and notes that more than 80% of economists surveyed by Bloomberg expect one at the Dec. 18 meeting.
opinion.why: 같은 통계에서 '헤드라인 숫자'와 '기초 추세'를 구분해 읽는 법을 배울 수 있다.
opinion.why_en: It teaches you to separate a flattering headline figure from the underlying trend in the same statistic.
